`send_message`, packaged: a blank @text@ with no @files@ posts nothing (a quiet protocol's silence);

dropping the FACT of it was not. The posted message's id is still not carried — a caller that needs it

declarations.documentation:
Serve a channel forever, delivering each incoming message to @deliver_to@ as one `message` value —
shaped like `time.watch` / `google_calendar.watch` so it composes under `parallel [ … ]`. Bot posts
(this bot's own replies included) are not delivered, so replying from @deliver_to@ cannot loop.
@author@ on the delivered message is the sender's raw Discord user id (a snowflake — an ENUMERABLE
numeric id, not a name); a plain digest of an enumerable id is dictionary-reversible, so pass it
through `author_tag` before letting it leave the program, e.g. as an AI provider's abuse-attribution
tag. That agent is this package's answer to a pseudonym every bot was otherwise writing (and getting
wrong) for itself: keyed with `crypto.hmac_sha256` under a named secret, so the tag cannot be walked
back to an account.

@display_name@ beside it is the name Discord SHOWS for that sender, and it is not a second identity: a
display name is SELF-CHOSEN and NOT UNIQUE — anyone in the server can set their nickname to read exactly
like the operator's, and a public channel is precisely where a stranger will. So a program that decides
what it may do from the name it was told has no authorization at all. Branch on @author@ (or on a tag
derived from it) and treat @display_name@ as what it is: how to ADDRESS the speaker.

Delivery is exactly once WITHIN one live gateway connection, and NOT GUARANTEED either way across a
reconnect — which is where this differs from the Slack twin's at-least-once. The gateway has no
per-event acknowledgement, so a message can be MISSED: an invalidated session, an outage past the
resume window, or this run restarting each re-identify, and Discord backfills nothing onto a fresh
session. A message can also be REPEATED, though far more rarely: a resume replays from the last
sequence the shard RECORDED, which it advances when an event ARRIVES rather than after @deliver_to@
returns. No dedup memory is kept here. A bot that must miss nothing reconciles against the channel's
own history rather than trusting this stream.

A runtime restart INTERRUPTS this call and costs nothing else, which is what changed in 0.7.0: the
token is the whole of what the sidecar needs, so a re-forked watch opens a new socket and serves the
same channel again. (0.6.0 handed the re-fork the opaque client handle it was still carrying, whose
client had died with the process, so every attempt panicked identically — a silent crash loop where a
plain `region.crashed` → fork again now works.) What the interruption costs is the messages that arrive
while nothing is watching, which is the reconnect gap above and not a new one.

It RAISES `discord_error` (`auth_error` | `api_error`) when the gateway will not open, because opening
it is now this call's job: `use discord.provider(...)` connects to nothing and so throws no
`discord_error` at all. An invalid token stops the watch as `auth_error` on its first attempt.

declarations.documentation:
Post @prompt@ with @controls@ as ONE message and BLOCK until someone in the channel COMPLETES one of
them, returning which control answered and with what — the human-in-the-loop step (approving an
irreversible action, editing a draft before it goes out, choosing among candidates, taking a note).
Those are not four agents: they are this call with different @controls@ data — two `button`s is an
approval, a `form` of one empty `field` is free-form text, a `form` of PREFILLED fields is draft
editing, a `select` is a pick from a computed list.

Ask in a channel whose MEMBERSHIP is the trust boundary: any member may answer, and the FIRST
COMPLETED interaction is the answer. Merely opening a form's dialog completes nothing, so a curious
click cannot consume the question. Once answered, the controls are stripped off the message and the
outcome left in their place, so the channel keeps a readable record and a late click has nothing to
press. A question that ends WITHOUT an answer is stripped the same way and left reading `(expired)`:
an expiry, a cancel or a teardown never abandons live controls in the channel for someone to press
into nothing. Stripping is best effort either way — if the edit itself fails the stale controls stay,
and clicking one gets Discord's own "interaction failed" notice.

What that record READS is the control's own text — a `button`'s or `form`'s @label@, a `select`'s
picked @option@ — so those strings are not merely what a human clicks: they become the channel's
lasting, public account of what was decided. Write them as the audit line you would want to find
later. The record names the answerer as a Discord MENTION (the channel renders it as a name), while
the @by@ the `answer` carries is the raw id — the readable form is for the channel, the correlatable
one for the program.

`ask` holds NO time limit, deliberately: a deadline is `time.with_deadline` wrapped around it and a
withdrawal is `region.cancel_by_id` on the fiber holding it. One blocking question composes with
both, whereas an expiry baked in here would make every caller handle a timeout it never asked for.

The wait rides one external call, so a runtime restart while it is open interrupts it under the
at-most-once rule (a catchable panic) and the controls already in the channel go stale — nothing is left
to strip them, so a late click gets Discord's own "interaction failed" notice. That is the DESIGNED
outcome, not a defect to absorb here: let the panic ride to your supervisor and ASK AGAIN — whoever
wanted the answer wants it still — rather than inventing an answer for an interaction that never landed.
Asking again is the whole recovery as of 0.7.0: the new ask resolves the token and opens its own socket,
with no connection left over from before to be dead.

Raises `discord_error` when a Discord call fails: opening the gateway (an invalid token is `auth_error`),
posting the question, or opening a form's dialog.

A control past one of Discord's caps splits two ways, and the split is what stops a cosmetic string
from being able to break a run. PRESENTATION is CLAMPED, never fatal: a `button`'s or `form`'s @label@
past 80 characters, a `select`'s @label@ past 150, a `form`'s @title@ past 45 and a `field`'s @label@
past 45 are shortened with a trailing `…`, and a BLANK one renders as the control's own @id@ (blank is
just as illegal to Discord as over-long, so it needs a substitute either way). What CARRIES MEANING is
CHECKED instead and fails the ask as `api_error`: an @id@ (at most 100 characters, 94 for a `form` —
it is the routing key, and two shortened ids could collide and answer the wrong control), a `select`
option (1 to 100 — the option's text IS the answer), and a `field`'s @value@ (at most 4000 — the draft
a human submits as approved). Whatever this package cannot check locally is still the platform
rejecting the payload and still `api_error`: a sixth row, a 26th option, a dialog past five fields.

RUN `check_controls` WHERE THE CONTROLS ARE BUILT, not here. It answers every one of those caps —
including the counts above and the duplicate @id@ neither side catches — as a VALUE, purely, with no
credential and no connection needed: a gate's constructor can refuse itself before a run ever starts.
It is not wired into this agent on purpose. `ask` returns an `answer` and has no room in that type for a verdict, so
an internal check could only THROW — and a cosmetic string that can throw is the exact failure this
package's clamping was written to remove. So the verdict stays a value, `ask` stays unchanged, and
what a failed check means is the caller's decision.

@by@ on the answer is the answerer's raw Discord user id (a snowflake — an ENUMERABLE numeric id, not
a name); a plain digest of an enumerable id is dictionary-reversible, so pass it through `author_tag`
before letting it leave the program. The @display_name@ beside
it is what that answerer is CALLED, and a name is SELF-CHOSEN and NOT UNIQUE — a channel's other
members can wear it too. A question whose answer depends on WHO gave it must read @by@; a name that
decided anything would let whoever renamed themselves decide it instead.

declarations.documentation:
Check @controls@ against Discord's caps LOCALLY and answer with a VALUE — `valid`, or `invalid`
carrying one sentence naming the offending control. Pure: no credential, no io, nothing to catch, so
it belongs where the controls are BUILT (a gate's constructor, a test) rather than where they are
asked.

It is deliberately NOT wired into `ask`, and that is the lesson of the outage this exists for. `ask`
returns an `answer`; there is no room in that type for a verdict, so an internal check could only
THROW — and a cosmetic string that can throw is exactly the failure mode this package spent a release
removing (a 67-character label once restarted a resident system on every attempt). So the check is a
separate agent whose result is data, `ask`'s behaviour is unchanged, and a caller decides what a
failed check means: refuse the gate, shorten the label, log and ask anyway.

What it reports is wider than what `ask` FAILS on, on purpose:

- FATAL, as `ask` would: a blank or over-long @id@, a blank or over-long `select` option, a dropdown
  with no options or past `limits`' @select_options@, a dialog with no boxes or past @form_fields@,
  an over-long `field` @value@, a control list that needs more than @rows@ rows, and an EMPTY
  @controls@ (a question nobody can answer, which Discord posts happily).
- SILENT, which `ask` survives and a program still wants to know: a label, placeholder or title past
  its cap is SHORTENED with an ellipsis, and a blank one renders as the control's own @id@ — so the
  channel's lasting record of what was decided reads as an internal key, or as most of a sentence.
- DUPLICATE ids, which nothing else catches at all. Two controls sharing an @id@ cannot be told apart
  on the way back: Discord returns the id and nothing more. The sidecar keeps the FIRST and warns, so
  pressing the second control completes the first control's answer — "deny" answering as "approve".
  A `form`'s @fields@ are checked the same way, since `submitted.values` is keyed by field id and two
  boxes sharing one would collapse into a single entry.

Lengths are counted in Unicode CODE POINTS while the renderer counts UTF-16 units, so an astral
character (an emoji outside the BMP) is one here and two there; a string within a character or two of
its cap should be shortened rather than argued about.

```katari
let controls = [discord.button(id = "approve", label = "approve"), discord.button(id = "deny", label = "deny")]
match (discord.check_controls(controls = controls)) {
  case discord.valid() -> discord.ask(channel = channel, prompt = prompt, controls = controls)
  case discord.invalid(reason => reason) -> refuse_to_open_the_gate(why = reason)
}
```

Discord caps a dropdown at 25 options of 100 characters, and renders @label@ as the placeholder line
shown while nothing is picked.

$katari_constructor.description: The tag that selects this variant. Write this exact string.

id.description: The answer's identity; returned verbatim as `chose.id`. At most 100 characters, and NOT shortened — see `button`'s @id@.

label.description: The placeholder line shown while nothing is picked; at most 150 characters, shortened with `…` beyond that. Blank leaves Discord's own default line in place.

options.description: The options offered; the picked one returns as `chose.option`. Each is 1 to 100 characters and is NOT shortened: the option's own text IS the answer, so a clamped one would report a choice the program never offered — an over-long or blank option fails the ask as `api_error`.

converges.

valid: The controls are askable exactly as written: every string fits, every count fits, every id is
distinct, and nothing would be shortened or substituted on the way to the channel.

declarations.documentation:
Shorten @text@ so it fits in ONE Discord message, ending it with @marker@ when anything was cut —
the arithmetic every caller was doing against `limits()` by hand, and the half of that job which is
mechanical rather than editorial.

WHY IT IS NOT MERELY A SLICE. Past `limits()`'s @message_text@ Discord REFUSES the post rather than
shortening it, so an over-long prompt is a question that can never be asked (a gate that can never be
granted, failing identically on every retry) and an over-long reply is a message that never lands. The
room is therefore @message_text@ MINUS the marker's own length, because the marker is part of what gets
posted — measuring the text, cutting it to the cap and appending afterwards is the one way this is got
wrong, and it puts the result back over the cap every time.

WHY THE MARKER IS YOURS. Only the caller knows what the reader needs told, but SOMETHING must be told:
text that was silently docked reads exactly like text that ended, and a model reading it will answer
from a fragment as though it had the whole. Write the marker as the FACT — "… (cut: the first 1,900 of
7,400 characters)" — rather than as a bare ellipsis, so whoever reads it knows to ask for the rest.

Text that already fits comes back UNCHANGED, with no marker, so this is safe to wrap around everything.
A @marker@ that alone exceeds the cap leaves no room for any text and comes back cut to the cap itself:
the one guarantee here is that the result fits.

Lengths are Katari code points and Discord counts UTF-16 units, so text within a couple of characters of
the cap should be given a longer marker rather than trusted to either count.

parameters.documentation: The text to fit; returned unchanged when it already does.

parameters.documentation: What to end the result with when anything was cut — your own words, saying that it was cut and ideally by how much.
parameters.label: marker

marker.description: What to end the result with when anything was cut — your own words, saying that it was cut and ideally by how much.

text.description: The text to fit; returned unchanged when it already does.

declarations.documentation:
Tag a Discord user id into a short, stable PSEUDONYM — the ~25 lines every bot that lets a speaker
reach a model or a log was writing for itself, with the same one way to get it wrong.

WHY NOT A PLAIN DIGEST. A snowflake is an ENUMERABLE numeric id: it is a timestamp, a worker, a
process and a counter, so the space a real id lives in is small enough to walk. `crypto.sha256` of
one is therefore reversible by dictionary — anyone holding the digest hashes candidate snowflakes
until one matches, and the pseudonym is a user id again. `crypto.hmac_sha256` under a secret KEY has
no such attack: without the key there is nothing to hash candidates with. That is the whole
difference between a pseudonym and an obfuscation, and it is one function call wide, which is exactly
why it kept being got wrong.

WHAT COMES OUT is safe to SHOW: @length@ hex characters (8 by default — 32 bits, opaque and short
enough to sit inline in a prompt or a log line), stable for as long as the key is, and meaningless to
anyone without the key. Rotating the key rotates every pseudonym, which is the intended way to sever
a correlation. Keep @length@ generous if the tag must be UNIQUE rather than merely readable: 8 hex
characters collide at around 2^16 distinct speakers by the birthday bound, so a full 64 is what a
program correlating abuse reports across a large server should carry, and a short one is what it
shows. The result is deliberately PUBLIC despite the private key — an HMAC reveals nothing about its
key, which is the sound declassification `crypto.hmac_sha256` documents.

THE KEY is named, not passed: a `credentials.source` (`credentials.env(key = ...)` or
`credentials.oauth(name = ...)`), so the secret's VALUE never enters the app's dataflow. It resolves
at EVERY call, like every other credential use in Katari, so a rotated key lands without a restart —
a bot tagging every message pays one credential read per message for that. Any secret with a stable
lifetime will do; the bot's own token is the usual choice, since it already exists and dies with the
bot's identity.

WHAT IT IS NOT is an anonymisation. A pseudonym is stable by construction, so it links everything one
person ever said; what it removes is the ability to turn that link back into an account. Whether even
a pseudonymous link may cross to an AI provider is the app's judgement, exactly as with
`display_name` — this agent only makes the tag correct.
declarations.name: author_tag

parameters.label: author

parameters.documentation: How many hex characters to keep, from 1 to 64 (the full tag); defaults to 8 — short enough to read, wide enough to tell a channel's speakers apart. Out of range is clamped into it.
parameters.label: length
